lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setting a goal you can measure
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a vague goal into a measurable one with a date.
This lesson builds toward: Given a vague training goal, you will rewrite it as one measurable goal with a number, a date and a test, with all four parts present and the goal agreed with your coach.
"Get faster" is a wish. "Run the 40-yard dash 0.1 seconds faster by the end of the preseason, timed the same way each time" is a goal you can measure.
A good training goal names one thing, a number, a date, and how it will be measured. It should be agreed with your coach so it fits the team plan.
An AI assistant can help you rewrite a vague goal. Try: "Turn my goal 'get stronger for soccer' into one measurable goal with a date. Ask me questions if you need more information."
Step by step:
- Write your goal in your own words.
- Add one number to measure.
- Add a date.
- Say how and when it will be tested.
- Agree it with your coach.
Words to know:
- Measurable: something you can count or time, so you know if it changed.
- Baseline: your starting number before you train for the goal.
Try it now: Write one vague goal. Ask an AI assistant to make it measurable with a date. Edit it so it is true to you, then write your baseline number if you know it.
You can now write a measurable training goal with a number, a date and a test.

check.q: Which part turns "get stronger" into a measurable goal?
options: Adding a number, a date and how it will be tested
check.why: A measurable goal names one thing, a number, a date and how it is measured.

check.q: You wrote a measurable goal with AI help. What do you do next?
options: Ask the AI to approve it
check.why: Your goal should be agreed with your coach so it fits the team plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Logging the right training data
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple training log that you will actually keep.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets, you will set up and keep a training log with Date, Session, Effort and Result, with a row filled in after every session for at least four sessions.
Data is only useful if you collect it the same way every time. A simple log beats a fancy app you stop using after a week.
Four columns are enough to start: Date, Session (what you did), Effort (how hard it felt, 1 to 10), and Result (the number for your goal). Some athletes add sleep hours or a short note.
Wearables like watches and heart-rate straps can add data, but they are not perfect. Treat their numbers as clues, not facts, and keep your health data private.
Step by step:
- Open Google Sheets.
- Make columns: Date, Session, Effort (1-10), Result.
- Fill one row after every session.
- Keep it in the same place on your phone so it takes one minute.
Words to know:
- Effort rating: a 1 to 10 score for how hard a session felt; coaches often call this RPE (rating of perceived exertion).
- Wearable: a device you wear, like a watch, that measures things like heart rate or steps.
Try it now: Create your training log in Google Sheets with the four columns. Fill in your last two or three sessions from memory or your notes.
You can now keep a simple, consistent training log.

check.q: What goes in the Result column of your log?
check.why: Result holds the number you are tracking for your goal.

check.q: You keep forgetting to fill in your log. What helps most?
options: Fill it once a month from memory
Keep it in the same place on your phone and fill one row right after each session
check.why: A simple log filled in the same way every time is the one you will keep.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading your training trend
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read a chart of your data and describe what it shows in one or two sentences.
This lesson builds toward: Given a chart of your own training log, you will describe the trend in one or two sentences and compare effort with result, naming the direction correctly and checking any AI math yourself.
After a few weeks, chart your Result column by date. Look at the direction: up, down or flat. One bad day does not mean much; look at the overall line.
Compare Effort and Result. If effort keeps going up but results stay flat or drop, you may be tired, and that is something to tell your coach.
You can paste your table (no names or health records) into an AI assistant and ask: "Describe the trend in this training data in plain words. What questions should I ask my coach?" Check its math yourself.
Step by step:
- Select Date and Result and insert a line chart.
- Say the direction: up, down or flat.
- Compare Effort with Result.
- Write a one-sentence summary.
Words to know:
- Trend: the overall direction of your numbers over time.
- Plateau: when results stop improving for a while.
Try it now: Chart your Result column. Write one sentence describing the trend. Then ask an AI assistant to describe it and compare its sentence with yours.
You can now chart your training data and describe the trend in plain words.

check.q: What do you look at first on your training chart?
options: The overall direction: up, down or flat
check.why: One bad day does not mean much; the overall line shows the trend.

check.q: You paste your table into an AI assistant. What do you remove first?
check.why: Keep names and health records out of AI tools.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using AI with your coach

lessons.title: Lesson 4: What AI can and cannot do for training
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Sort training tasks into ones AI can help with and ones that belong to your coach or athletic trainer.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of training tasks, you will identify which tasks AI can help with and which belong to your coach or athletic trainer, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
AI assistants are good at organizing: turning notes into a table, explaining a training term, summarizing your log, or writing questions for your coach.
They are not good at knowing your body. They cannot see your form, your injury history or how you slept, and general plans from the internet may not fit your age, level or season.
So use AI to understand and prepare, and let your coach and athletic trainer decide your workouts, loads and return from injury.
Words to know:
- Training load: how much and how hard you train over time.
- Athletic trainer: a licensed health professional who prevents, treats and helps athletes recover from injuries.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain one training word you have heard (for example "periodization" or "deload week") in simple words. Write one question about it for your coach.
You can now say which training tasks AI can help with and which belong to your coach or athletic trainer.

check.q: Which of these can an AI assistant do well for training?
check.why: AI is good at organizing and explaining, not at knowing your body.

check.q: An AI assistant gives you a heavier lifting plan than your coach wrote. What do you do?
options: Use it to prepare a question and let your coach decide
check.why: Use AI to understand and prepare; your coach decides workouts and loads.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting unsafe AI training advice
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize red flags in AI or online training advice.
This lesson builds toward: Given AI or online training advice, you will identify red flags such as training through pain, cutting water or risky supplements, spotting every red flag and taking it to your coach or athletic trainer instead of following it.
AI and online plans can give advice that is too much, too fast, or wrong for young or injured athletes. You need to spot it.
Red flags: training through sharp pain; big jumps in training all at once; cutting food or water to make weight; supplements promising fast results; "no rest days"; and any plan that ignores what your coach wrote.
Supplements are a special risk: they are not checked by the FDA before they are sold, and some contain banned substances. Talk with your athletic trainer or a registered dietitian before taking any.
Step by step:
- Read the advice slowly.
- Check it against the red-flag list.
- If any red flag appears, do not follow it.
- Take it to your coach or athletic trainer.
Words to know:
- Red flag: a warning sign that something is unsafe or wrong.
- Supplement: a pill, powder or drink sold to add something to your diet.
Official sources:
- USADA: Supplement Connect (supplement risks for athletes)
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for "a plan to get faster in two weeks". Read it and circle any red flags. Write what you would ask your coach about it.
You can now spot unsafe training advice and take it to the right person.

check.q: Which of these is a red flag in training advice?
options: A plan that matches what your coach wrote
Big jumps in training all at once
check.why: Too much, too fast is one of the red flags in the lesson.

check.q: A teammate shares a supplement that promises fast results. What do you do?
options: Talk to your athletic trainer or a registered dietitian first
Buy it if the reviews are good
Ask the AI to approve it
check.why: Supplements are not checked by the FDA before sale and some contain banned substances.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Preparing a training talk with your coach
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to prepare a short, clear update and three questions for your coach.
This lesson builds toward: Using your goal, your log and an AI assistant, you will write a three-sentence coach update and three questions about your next training block, in your own words, with no health records shared and your coach's answer used to update your plan.
Coaches are busy. A short, clear update with your numbers makes the conversation better: what your goal is, what your data shows, and what you want to ask.
Ask an AI assistant: "Here is my goal and my training log. Write a three-sentence update for my coach and suggest three questions I could ask about my next training block." Then edit it so it sounds like you.
Bring the update to your coach in person or in the way your team prefers. Listen, take notes, and update your plan with what your coach says, not what the AI said.
Step by step:
- Paste your goal and log (no health records).
- Ask for a three-sentence update and three questions.
- Edit it in your own words.
- Share it with your coach the way your team prefers.
- Update your plan with your coach's answer.
Words to know:
- Training block: a set of weeks with one main training focus.
- Update: a short message that says where you are now.
Try it now: Final task: log at least four sessions, ask an AI assistant to describe your trend, and write a three-sentence update with three questions for your coach.
You can now turn your training data into a clear update and questions for your coach.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Measurable goal The goal is vague, or a number, date or test is missing. One thing, a number, a date and a test, agreed with the coach. Includes a baseline number and fits a named part of the team's season plan. Training log Fewer than four sessions, or columns are missing. Date, Session, Effort and Result filled in for at least four sessions. Every session logged the same day, with a short note or sleep hours added. Trend summary No chart, or the direction is wrong or missing. A chart and a one- or two-sentence summary of the direction, with effort compared to result and the AI's math checked. Spots a plateau or rising effort with flat results and flags it as a question for the coach. Safe use of AI Follows or repeats advice with a red flag, or shares health records with AI. No red-flag advice is followed, and anything doubtful is taken to the coach or athletic trainer. Names the specific red flag and why it is unsafe when raising it. Coach questions Fewer than three questions, or the update reads as copied AI text. A three-sentence update and three clear questions in the athlete's own words. The athlete records the coach's answers and updates the plan from them. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What three things does a good coach update cover?
options: Your goal, what your data shows and what you want to ask
Your social media, sleep and grades
check.why: A short update gives your goal, your data and your questions.

check.q: Your coach's answer differs from the AI's suggestion. What do you do?
options: Update your plan with what your coach said
check.why: Update your plan with your coach's answer, not what the AI said.
